prompt: Why does this course recommend a virtual machine over installing on your own computer?
hint: Think about what makes your numbers comparable with the lesson's.

choices.text: A VM runs PyTorch faster than an installed Python
choices.why: It is slower if anything, and with a graphics card installed is the faster path.

choices.text: It matches the recording machine, and is disposable
choices.why: Right. A difference in your output is then the processor's arithmetic, not the setup, and a broken environment costs nothing.

choices.text: A VM sees the graphics card directly
choices.why: It does not, which is why the installed path is the one for a computer with an NVIDIA card.

choices.text: PyTorch only publishes packages for Linux
choices.why: It publishes them for Windows and macOS too; the lesson says what each one uses.

prompt: The check prints `2.14.1+cu130 False`. What does the `False` tell you?
hint: Two separate facts sit on that line.

choices.text: The installation failed and has to be repeated
choices.why: The import worked and printed a version, so the installation is fine.

choices.text: The package was built without CUDA
choices.why: `+cu130` says it was built against CUDA 13.0. The build has it; the machine has no card to use it on.

choices.text: PyTorch found no graphics card to run on
choices.why: Right, and on a VM that is the expected answer. Everything in the course runs on the processor.

choices.text: The virtual environment is not active in this terminal
choices.why: Without it, `import torch` would have failed before printing anything.

prompt: Most of the 5.7 GB environment is code for NVIDIA cards, on a machine with no card. What is the smaller alternative the lesson names?
hint: PyTorch publishes more than one build.

choices.text: Deleting the `nvidia` folders after installing
choices.why: PyTorch imports them at start-up, so removing them by hand breaks the import.

choices.text: Installing an older PyTorch
choices.why: Older builds carry CUDA libraries too, and the course's versions would no longer match.

choices.text: The processor-only build, from PyTorch's own package index
choices.why: Right. On a VM it computes the same results; it was not run for this course because its machine could not reach that index.

choices.text: Skipping torchvision
choices.why: torchvision is small next to the CUDA libraries, and lessons 12 and 13 need it.

prompt: A new terminal prints `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'torch'`, though the installation finished. What is the first thing to check?
hint: Where was torch installed?

choices.text: `which python`
choices.why: Right. If it is not the one inside `~/dl/.venv`, this terminal never activated the environment.

choices.text: Whether the disk is full
choices.why: A full disk stops the installation itself, with its own message; this one finished.

choices.text: Whether the machine has a graphics card
choices.why: PyTorch imports without a card and reports `False`; the card never stops an import.

choices.text: Whether `pip install torch` should be run with `--break-system-packages`
choices.why: That installs into the system's own Python, which the lesson says to leave alone.

prompt: You rerun a lesson's program on your VM and get 0.951 where the lesson printed 0.956. What does that most likely mean?
hint: The seed is fixed. What else can differ between two machines?

choices.text: Your copy of the data is different
choices.why: The digits ship inside scikit-learn, and the split uses a fixed seed: every machine has the same images in the same sets.

choices.text: Rounding in a different order on a different processor
choices.why: Right. Over thousands of steps a last-digit difference becomes a second-decimal one. The shape is what to compare.

choices.text: The environment is broken and needs reinstalling
choices.why: A broken environment fails to import or to run, not by half a point.

choices.text: The seed is ignored on machines without a graphics card
choices.why: The seed is honoured on the processor; the lesson's own machine has no card.

prompt: How many images does `digits.load()` put in the training set?
hint: The first line `look.py` printed.

prompt: Why does `digits.py` divide every pixel by 16?
hint: What is the largest value a pixel has in the raw data?

choices.text: To make the images 16 times smaller
choices.why: The image stays 64 numbers; only their scale changes.

choices.text: To put every input between 0 and 1
choices.why: Right: ink is stored as 0 to 16, and inputs on a small common scale train more smoothly.

choices.text: Because PyTorch refuses integers as input
choices.why: The conversion to float is `astype`, a separate step; and these lessons use NumPy until lesson 9.

choices.text: To turn the image into black and white
choices.why: The grey levels survive as fractions; nothing is thresholded.

prompt: A colleague tunes the number of hidden units by trying ten values and keeping the one with the best test accuracy. What is wrong with the 0.97 they report?
hint: What is each set for?

choices.text: Nothing, since test data was never used for training
choices.why: The weights never saw it, but the choice of setting did, and the choice is part of the model.

choices.text: It was chosen on the test set, so it overstates
choices.why: Right. Validation is where settings are picked; test, looked at once, is what estimates the result on new data.

choices.text: Ten values are too few to choose from
choices.why: More values would make the leak worse, not better.

choices.text: Accuracy is the wrong metric for ten balanced classes
choices.why: With every digit between 92 and 121 times, accuracy is a fair measure here.

prompt: What does the perceptron's learning rule change when the unit answers correctly?
hint: Look at the `if`.

choices.text: It makes the weights a little larger
choices.why: Only a mistake moves them.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right. The update sits inside `if out != target`.

choices.text: It resets the bias to zero
choices.why: The bias moves only on a mistake, like the weights.

choices.text: It halves the size of the next update
choices.why: The rule has no step size that changes; every update is plus or minus the input.

prompt: Why did the perceptron still get XOR wrong after twenty epochs?
hint: What shape is the boundary of one unit?

choices.text: Twenty epochs was too few; a few hundred would do it
choices.why: No number of epochs helps: there is no set of weights that gets all four right.

choices.text: The step function is too steep to learn with
choices.why: It learnt AND with the same function in six epochs.

choices.text: No straight line separates XOR's 1s from its 0s
choices.why: Right. One unit draws one line, and XOR's classes sit on opposite diagonals.

choices.text: The bias started at zero
choices.why: It started at zero for AND as well, and the rule moves it.

prompt: A single unit separates its inputs with a straight ___, which is why it can learn AND and not XOR.
hint: A boundary in the plane of two inputs.

prompt: Match each activation to what it does to a large positive sum such as 3.
hint: The `activations.py` table, last column.

prompt: What is the problem with a sigmoid unit whose sum is far from zero, at -10 or +10?
hint: What happens to the output when the sum moves a little there?

choices.text: Its output leaves the range 0 to 1
choices.why: Sigmoid never leaves 0 to 1, whatever the sum.

choices.text: The curve is flat, so a change in the sum barely changes the output
choices.why: Right, and a unit whose output does not respond to its sum gets almost no signal to train with.

choices.text: It becomes a dead unit and outputs zero for every input
choices.why: That is ReLU's weakness on its negative side; sigmoid at +10 outputs nearly 1.

choices.text: It costs more to compute
choices.why: It costs the same at any input; the problem is the slope.

prompt: A ReLU unit's sum turned negative for every training image after an unlucky update. What happens to it from then on?
hint: What does ReLU pass back for a negative sum?

choices.text: It recovers on the next batch
choices.why: It outputs zero for every input, so no batch gives it a reason to change.

choices.text: It saturates near 1 like a sigmoid
choices.why: ReLU has no ceiling; on the negative side it is exactly 0.

choices.text: It starts outputting negative values
choices.why: ReLU cuts every negative to zero; that is all it does.

choices.text: It stays at zero: a dead unit
choices.why: Right. Leaky ReLU and GELU give the negative side a small slope so that this cannot happen.

prompt: A layer takes 64 inputs and has 32 units. How many parameters does it have, counting the biases?
hint: One weight per input per unit, and one bias per unit.

prompt: A batch of 5 images of 64 pixels goes into a layer of 16 units. What is the shape of the result?
hint: The inner numbers of a product cancel.

choices.why: That is the weight matrix, the same whatever the batch.
The rows stay the images: `(5, 64) @ (64, 16)` keeps 5 rows.
Right: one row per image, one column per unit.
That is the input; a layer of 16 units gives 16 numbers per image.

prompt: A network has three layers of 64, 32 and 10 units with nothing between them. What can it compute that a single 64-to-10 layer cannot?
hint: `layer.py`'s last line.

choices.text: Anything a single layer of 32 units could
choices.why: Without an activation the stack merges into one product, whatever the widths.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right. The weight matrices multiply into one 64 by 10 matrix; the extra layers add parameters and no ability.

choices.text: XOR-like problems, since it has more than one layer
choices.why: Depth helps only with an activation between the layers; xor.py's step is what made it work.

choices.text: Problems that need more than 10 outputs
choices.why: The output width is 10 in both.

prompt: Put the computation `xor.py` does for one input in order.
hint: The output unit reads the hidden ones.
items: Multiply the two inputs by W1 and add b1
Apply the step: the OR unit and the AND unit fire or not
Multiply the two hidden outputs by W2 and add b2
Apply the step: 1 only for OR without AND

prompt: The universal approximation theorem says one hidden layer can approximate any continuous function. Why are practical networks deeper anyway?
hint: What does the theorem not promise?

choices.text: The theorem was disproved for ReLU networks
choices.why: It holds for ReLU; what it leaves out is the cost.

choices.text: A single hidden layer cannot have more than a few hundred units
choices.why: There is no such limit; the problem is how many the function needs.

choices.text: It promises nothing about how many units, or whether training finds them
choices.why: Right. Deeper networks reach the same function with far fewer parameters, and training finds it.

choices.text: Deep networks need no activation function
choices.why: Without one, any depth collapses to a single layer.
